Goblet
GOB-let
n. (a round drinking bowl without a handle)
From Old French gobelet, a small cup. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the Song, in the bridegroom's description of his bride.

Biblical Definition

Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies. The Song of Solomon is a canonical book of married love, and its frankness is deliberate. The dictionary takes it in the plain sense first — a husband praising his wife's body in language of plenty, a cup that is never empty and a harvest heap ringed with flowers — and then in the covenantal sense the whole book carries, since Scripture uses marriage from Genesis to Revelation as the figure of Christ and his church. The book's own summary of the relation is the line the bride speaks a few verses later: I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me. That belonging is mutual, exclusive, and delighted, and it is the same shape as the covenant. Proverbs gives the plain counsel in the same register: let thy fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of thy youth. And Paul gives the command that governs a Christian husband and sets the cost of it: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a kind of cup or drinking vessel, without a handle; in Scripture, the bridegroom's figure in the Song of Solomon.

GOBLET, n. A kind of cup or drinking vessel, without a handle.

BRIDEGROOM, n. A man newly married; or a man about to be married.

SPOUSE, n. A man or woman engaged or joined in wedlock; a married person.

CONJUGAL, a. Belonging to marriage; suitable or appropriate to the marriage state.

TYPE, n. A sign; a symbol; a figure of something to come.

Key Scripture

Sng 7:2 — "Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies."

Sng 7:10 — "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me."

Pro 5:18 — "Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth."

Eph 5:25 — "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;"

Modern Corruption

The Song is either allegorised until nothing bodily remains in it, or read as a celebration of desire detached from covenant; it is a canonical book about a husband and a wife, and about Christ and the church, and it will not release either sense.

expand to see more

The older allegorising tradition was embarrassed by the book and read every line as doctrine with no marriage left in it. The modern reading keeps the body and drops the covenant, taking the Song as a celebration of erotic feeling as such. Both lose something the text insists on. The Song is unmistakably about a man and a woman, and it is placed in a canon where marriage is from the first the joining of one man and one woman into one flesh, and where the prophets and the apostles use that union as the figure of God and his people. Ephesians 5 quotes Genesis 2:24 and says outright, this is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.

Taken this way the book preaches to husbands harder than it flatters them. The love commanded in Ephesians is measured by a cross — even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it — and the headship it establishes is therefore a headship of self-expenditure, not of convenience. The dictionary holds the complementarian order Scripture teaches and holds with it the delight the Song teaches, and refuses the caricature that treats the first as incompatible with the second. Let thy fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'aggan (H101), a bowl or basin; mezeg (H4197), mixed wine or liquor; teshuwqah (H8669), desire or longing.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'aggan (H101) — a bowl, a basin; rendered goblet at Song 7:2.

Hebrew mezeg (H4197) — mixture, mingled wine; which wanteth not liquor.

Hebrew teshuwqah (H8669) — a longing, a desire; his desire is toward me.

Hebrew dowd (H1730) — a beloved one, love; I am my beloved's.

Greek musterion (G3466) — a mystery, a thing once hidden now revealed; this is a great mystery.

Usage

"“Thy navel is like a round goblet” — the single occurrence."

"“rejoice with the wife of thy youth” — the same doctrine in Proverbs."

"“even as Christ also loved the church” — the measure set for a husband."
